title: Event Stream Partitioning Under Skewed Key Distribution: Rebalancing Mechanics, Consumer Lag, and the Hot Partition Trap
description: How skewed partition keys collapse Kafka throughput, why rebalancing amplifies lag, and the architectural decisions that prevent it in Go services.
linkedin_post:
Most Kafka lag problems are misdiagnosed.

Engineers see consumer group lag spiking and immediately reach for horizontal scaling—adding more consumer replicas. But if you're hitting a hot partition, more consumers don't help. A single partition is consumed by exactly one consumer. You can scale to 100 replicas; 98 of them will idle while one falls further behind.

Hot partitions happen when key distribution is skewed: a single tenant ID, a dominant device, a bot-heavy user cohort. The Kafka partitioner hashes the key and routes consistently to the same partition. High produce volume on that key means high lag on that partition—and the consumer assigned to it is drowning while adjacent consumers are underutilized.

It gets worse during rebalancing. A consumer under load can miss heartbeats if its poll interval stretches. The broker treats it as dead, triggers a rebalance, and the hot partition gets reassigned—usually to another similarly provisioned consumer. Lag accumulates through the rebalance window. The feedback loop compounds.

What actually helps:

→ Per-partition lag metrics, not aggregate group lag. Aggregate numbers hide skew behind healthy averages.

→ Decouple fetch and processing goroutines in your Go consumers. If processing blocks the poll loop, you're racing against session timeout on every slow message batch.

→ Key salting distributes a hot key across multiple partitions—but at the cost of per-key ordering guarantees. Only valid if your workload tolerates out-of-order processing.

→ Consumer-side rate limiting controls downstream write pressure even when the consumer can drain quickly. Sometimes the right move is to accept lag and protect MongoDB or Redis from saturation.

→ Increasing partition count only helps when lag is uniform. If two partitions are saturated and ten are idle, you don't have a parallelism problem—you have a key distribution problem.

The diagnostic question before any intervention: is the binding constraint the key distribution, the consumer processing speed, the downstream capacity, or the partition count? Each has a different lever. Pulling the wrong one wastes weeks.
